## 1. The subdomain list

> Here are the 12 subdomains under `chemistry-materials`. What is missing? What is a distinction nobody in your field actually makes? What are we calling by the wrong name?

(03 §12.2, ask 1.) The family: Benchmarks whose subject is a molecule, material, reaction or catalyst.

- Included: Tag this as PRIMARY if the scored quantity is a property, structure or behaviour of matter at the molecular or crystalline scale, whatever method produces it.
- Excluded: Do NOT tag this if the subject is a physical process rather than a substance, which is \`physics\`. The family is named for both communities deliberately: method does not decide the home, subject does, so a DFT-grounded materials benchmark is chemistry-materials and a quantum-simulation benchmark is physics. Do NOT tag it either where a small molecule is scored for how it binds a protein, as a bound pose or a predicted affinity, which is \`biology-genetics\` (\`protein-ligand-cofolding\`, \`drug-target-interaction\`). Compounds nominated and then assayed stay here, in \`experimental-hit-finding\`, because the experiment on the compound is the ground truth.

### 2.1 MoleculeNet (moleculenet)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/moleculenet.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*17 molecular property datasets, from DFT energies to clinical toxicity, each with a recommended split and metric.*

A benchmark collection for molecular machine learning, released with DeepChem by a Stanford group: 17 public datasets in four categories, quantum mechanics (QM7, QM7b, QM8, QM9), physical chemistry (ESOL, FreeSolv, Lipophilicity), biophysics (PCBA, MUV, HIV, PDBbind, BACE) and physiology (BBBP, Tox21, ToxCast, SIDER, ClinTox), over 700,000 compounds and over 800 tasks in all. A system takes a molecule, as SMILES or, for the quantum sets and PDBbind, 3D coordinates, and predicts each of the dataset's properties. For each dataset the paper recommends a split, 80/10/10 random, scaffold, time or stratified, and a metric, MAE or RMSE for regression and ROC-AUC or PRC-AUC for classification, averaged over a dataset's tasks; there is no score across datasets. The quantum labels are DFT and TDDFT/CC2 calculations, the rest mostly experimental measurements. The DeepChem loaders now default to scaffold splits for most datasets, and the documentation's recommended split differs from the paper's for ESOL, Lipophilicity, MUV and PDBbind, so a number means little without its split. A leaderboard repository last changed in 2021; results appear in papers.

#### moleculenet · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary chemistry-materials/molecular-property-prediction; secondary chemistry-materials/drug-discovery-admet, biology-genetics/drug-target-interaction · [S2][moleculenet-s2]
  - why: Every dataset scores a property of a molecule predicted from its structure, at four levels from quantum-mechanical energies to effects on the human body.
  > These properties can be subdivided into four categories: quantum mechanics, physical chemistry, biophysics and physiology.
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S2][moleculenet-s2]
  - why: Systems predict molecular properties and are scored against measurements or, for the quantum sets, DFT calculations.
  > Molecular machine learning methods have to be capable of learning to predict this very broad range of properties.
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S2][moleculenet-s2]
  - why: The scaffold split puts molecules with different two-dimensional frameworks in test than in training, and PDBbind's time split tests on newer complexes than it trains on. The paper recommends scaffold splits for HIV, BACE and BBBP and reports them as their own condition; the other datasets' recommended splits are random or stratified (review\_checks).
  > Three datasets (HIV, BACE, BBBP) in these two categories are evaluated under scaffold splitting.
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit, classification-metric · [S2][moleculenet-s2]
  - why: Regression datasets are scored by MAE or RMSE, classification datasets by ROC-AUC or PRC-AUC (PRC-AUC where positives are under 2%), each averaged over a dataset's tasks.
  > regression datasets are evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE) and root-mean-square error (RMSE)
- `designed_for_subjects` = scientific-surrogate-model · [S2][moleculenet-s2]
  - why: The entrants are models trained on each dataset's training split to stand in for the DFT calculation or the laboratory measurement that produced its labels; the paper frames the quantum sets as learning fast approximators to DFT, and compares FreeSolv models with alchemical free-energy calculations.
  > As most conventional methods are slower than data-driven methods by orders of magnitude

### 2.2 USPTO-MIT (uspto-mit)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/uspto-mit.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Forward reaction prediction on about 480,000 US-patent reactions, scored by top-k accuracy of the predicted product.*

The forward reaction prediction set built for its release paper, a NIPS 2017 paper on Weisfeiler-Lehman networks: about 480,000 reactions from US granted patents, taken from a public text-mined extraction with duplicates and erroneous reactions removed, atom-mapped, without stereochemistry, and split into training, development and test sets (409,035, 30,000 and 40,000 reactions in the distributed files; the paper rounds them to 400K, 40K and 40K). Given a reaction's reactants and reagents, a system predicts its product, and is scored by top-k accuracy, the share of test reactions whose recorded product is among its k highest-ranked predictions. Later papers call the set USPTO\_MIT or USPTO-480k. The Molecular Transformer paper (2019) added a mixed setting, with no split between reactants and reagents in the input, beside the separated setting earlier work used, which it argues presumes knowledge of the product; numbers from the two settings are not comparable. The release paper also had ten chemists predict 80 test reactions, on which its model scored 69.1% top-1 and the best chemist 72.0%. There is no leaderboard; results appear in the papers that use the set.

### 2.3 PaRoutes (paroutes)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/paroutes.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Multi-step retrosynthesis on two sets of 10,000 patent routes, scored by recovery of the patent's route in the top n.*

A framework for benchmarking multi-step retrosynthesis (route prediction) from AstraZeneca's Molecular AI group. Routes were extracted from reaction networks within US patents (a curated USPTO subset), and two sets of 10,000 diverse, non-overlapping routes were selected: set-n1 (one route per patent before the overlap check, shaped like the full pool) and set-n5 (five per patent, longer and richer in convergent routes). Each set comes with its target molecules, a stock made of all the reference routes' leaves (the stop criterion for the search), and a USPTO subset with the reference reactions removed for training one-step models. A planner returns routes as trees of molecules and reactions; the harness ranks them with a fixed route score, computes the tree edit distance to the patent's route, and reports top-1, top-5 and top-10 accuracy (a distance of zero within the first n ranks), the number of solved targets, and route diversity as the number of clusters an LSTM distance model forms. No aggregate is published. Version 2.0 (November 2022) re-extracted the routes and stocks from a re-processed USPTO set and keeps the set names; the maintainers' 2.0 results table was corrected in August 2024.

**Evidence** (48 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### paroutes · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  > We introduce a framework for benchmarking multi-step retrosynthesis methods, i.e. route predictions, called PaRoutes.
- `released` = 2022-02-25 · [S2][paroutes-s2]
  > "publication\_date": "2022-02-25"
- `release_venue` = Digital Discovery (Royal Society of Chemistry), 2022 · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  > Cite this: Digital Discovery, 2022, 1, 527

#### paroutes · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary chemistry-materials/retrosynthesis · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: The leaf is a route from a target back to purchasable starting materials, and that is PaRoutes' item exactly; the stock of each set stands in for the purchasable compounds, and the whole route, not one disconnection, is scored. USPTO-50k sits on the same leaf under ADR-0020's deferral of a single-step leaf; PaRoutes needs no such note.
  > One particular area of CASP is retrosynthesis analysis in which the aim is to predict the necessary steps to synthesize a compound, i.e. a synthetic route
- `capability` = planning · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: A route is a sequence of reactions that reaches a goal state, a tree whose leaves are all in stock, and the score is a property of that sequence as a whole (its distance to the patent's route, and whether its leaves are in stock), which is the term's test. The paper frames the task as building the steps recursively until the stop conditions hold.
  > The precursors produced by the one-step retrosynthesis can then be further broken down recursively until a set of conditions are met.
- `capability` = search-exploration · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: The paper's metric set rewards how the search covered the space as well as where it ended, with the number of distinct route clusters as the diversity measure, beside search time to convergence and solved targets under a fixed iteration budget.
  > the optimal number of clusters is viewed as a metric of diversity
- `evaluation_method` = exact-match, model-derived-metric · [S3][paroutes-s3]
  - why: Top-n accuracy gives each target a verdict, right only if a predicted route has a tree edit distance of zero to the reference route within the first n ranks, and averages them; route\_quality.py tests the distance against 1e-6 and takes the mean of best-n equal to 0. The diversity metric is the number of clusters formed from distances that a released LSTM model (chembl\_10k\_route\_distance\_model.ckpt, trained on routes for 10,000 ChEMBL compounds) computes in place of TED, so the checkpoint is part of that number.
  > topn = (stats\[f"best-{rank}"\] == 0).mean()
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model, classical-algorithm · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: The paper's entrants are search algorithms (MCTS, Retro\*, DFPN) driving a template-based one-step model trained on the provided USPTO subset, a model built for a task chemistry defines; the framework is also written for expert systems not derived from data, which use only the targets and stock, and a hand-coded rule system with no learned part is what classical-algorithm takes.
  > If your one-step model is an expert system not derived from big-data extraction, you should be able to use the provided targets and stock, and not consider the provided reaction datasets.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `chemistry-materials/reaction-prediction` · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: That leaf is the forward direction, products from reactants. PaRoutes works backwards from the target, and a forward model appears only in a 2026 paper's post-hoc check of its routes (Rachel), not in the protocol.
  > The precursors produced by the one-step retrosynthesis can then be further broken down recursively until a set of conditions are met.
- `capability` not `scientific-prediction` · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: The reference route is one recorded human choice, not a property of the target molecule; the authors say other routes may be as good and only synthesis could tell, so recovering the patent's route measures planning against a recorded plan, not the prediction of a chemical quantity.
  > but the only way to determine that is to perform the synthesis in the lab, which is not practically feasible for large numbers of routes.
- `capability` not `hypothesis-generation` · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: The output is a ranked set of candidate routes, but top-n asks only whether the one recorded route is in it, and the cluster count measures the set's spread, not whether its routes are worth making; search-exploration carries the spread.
  > we therefore limit the search problem to recovering the one route for each target that we have knowledge about.
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: Set-n5 is harder than set-n1 (longer, more convergent routes), but the paper presents it as a harder set from the same patents, not as a shifted condition beside a matched one.
  > Set-n5 consisting of a diverse set of 10 000 routes that are longer and enriched in convergent routes.
- `evaluation_method` not `domain-metric` · [S3][paroutes-s3]
  - why: The tree edit distance between routes is specific to synthesis planning, but the accuracy uses only whether it is zero, an identity test on the route tree; its magnitude is not reported. The README's leaves-overlap and route-length columns are diagnostics, not headline metrics.
  > if dist \< 1e-6:
- `evaluation_method` not `constraint-check` · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: A target counts as solved when a route's leaves are all in stock, but the harness reads that from the in\_stock flags the entrant's software writes into its routes, and the paper leaves both the timing and the solved check to that software; nothing in PaRoutes validates the route against a battery.
  > We consider the calculation of timings and if targets are solved to be part of the
- `evaluation_method` not `composite` · [S1][paroutes-s1]
  - why: The metrics are reported side by side and the paper argues against one number.
  > Relying on a single metric would be vulnerable to adversarial strategies and therefore we will suggest a set of complementary evaluation metrics.

- `task` = exists true; input a target molecule as a SMILES string (n1-targets.txt or n5-targets.txt), the set's stock molecules as SMILES (n1-stock.txt or n5-stock.txt), the stop criterion for the search, optionally, the curated USPTO subset without the reference reactions, for training a one-step model; output Routes for each target as JSON trees of molecule nodes (SMILES, an optional in\_stock flag) and featureless reaction nodes.; scoring The harness ranks each target's routes with a fixed route score (leaf cost 1 in stock and 10 out of it, reaction cost 1), so several routes can share a rank, then computes the tree edit distance of each to the reference route. Top-n accuracy is the share of targets with a route at distance zero among the first n ranks (n = 1, 5, 10). Solved targets counts targets with a route whose leaves are all in stock; diversity is the median number of route clusters.; tests_hidden_from_system false · [S1][paroutes-s1]

**Open review checks** (10):

1. (field `versions`) 2.0 is modelled as an edition (new items on the same task) because only about 14% of its targets are 1.0's, but the counting is this curator's (line comparison of the Zenodo files), not a quoted statement, and both releases fall in 2022 rather than in a new year. The maintainers call 2.0 a version; if a reviewer reads a re-extraction by the same maintainer as a revision, the version\_kind changes but breaking stays true. · [S8][paroutes-s8]
   > PaRoutes 2.0 reference routes and stocks.
2. (field `versions`) The 2024-08-05 correction of the README's 2.0 table is recorded as an erratum on 2.0, but it changes the maintainers' baselines, not the items. DirectMultiStep (2025) compares against the pre-correction figures. A reviewer should check whether an erratum, a history event or a ResultClaim correction is the right home. · [S4][paroutes-s4]
   > Table 3: Top-K accuracy on route test set-n1 (10 000 routes). Top-1 0.17 0.15 0.11
3. (field `evaluation_method`) exact-match was kept although the comparison is a tree edit distance of zero, which goes beyond the term's whitespace-or-case normalisation (as with USPTO-50k's InChI comparison); domain-metric is the other reading, if TED is taken as the metric rather than the identity test on it. · [S3][paroutes-s3]
   > if dist \< 1e-6:
4. (field `comparability`) The facets resolve to llm-static-text (exact-match with domain-specialist-model) and fallback, as for USPTO-50k; no profile fits a planner whose search budget, one-step training data and extra inputs are the material conditions. max\_steps (for the iteration budget) and eligibility\_track (for extra inputs) are stretches of those fields.
5. (field `capability`) capability is planning and search-exploration; hypothesis-generation was rejected although the cluster count scores the set of candidate routes. A reviewer may weigh it against search-exploration. · [S1][paroutes-s1]
   > the optimal number of clusters is viewed as a metric of diversity
6. (field `designed_for_subjects`) designed\_for\_subjects keeps classical-algorithm on the paper's invitation to expert systems; all of the paper's own entrants carry a learned one-step model. agent-scaffold was rejected for tree search, and Rachel's LLM planner is under observed\_subjects only. · [S1][paroutes-s1]
   > If your one-step model is an expert system not derived from big-data extraction, you should be able to use the provided targets and stock, and not consider the provided reaction datasets.
7. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk high follows USPTO-50k. It could be medium, since PaRoutes ships a training subset without the reference reactions and the risk is each entrant's training choice (training\_data\_policy).
8. (field `data.size`) The paper's stock sizes (13,633 and 13,783) differ from the 1.0 Zenodo files' line counts (13,647 and 13,798), and the 2.0 stocks (13,432 and 13,328) are quoted by no source. The 2.0 sizes and the \~450k pool come from the data README and file counts only.
9. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence is CC-BY-4.0 from both Zenodo records; DirectMultiStep describes the 2.0 route data as Apache 2.0, the repository's code licence. The upstream USPTO extraction's licence was not read. · [S4][paroutes-s4]
   > The reaction route dataset is from the 2.0 version of PaRoutes in their GitHub repository \[44\], available under the Apache License 2.0.
10. (field `curation.sources`) The paper was read through a Wayback capture of the publisher's PDF, which drops the fi, fl and ft ligatures in its text layer; the ChemRxiv preprint and the ESI (pseudo-code, the cross-comparison tables) were not read. Rachel's PaRoutes120 does not state which PaRoutes version its targets come from.

**Reviewer checklist** for `paroutes`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.4 MOSES (moses)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/moses.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Distribution-learning benchmark for molecular generation, on a 1.9M-molecule ZINC Clean Leads set with eleven metrics.*

An open-source Python platform (the molsets package) that standardises the distribution-learning half of molecular generation: a model is trained on one prescribed dataset, samples at least 30,000 molecules, and the package scores the valid ones against a held-out reference set. The dataset is ZINC Clean Leads filtered to 1.9M molecules and split into train, a random test set and a scaffold test set whose Bemis-Murcko scaffolds appear in neither of the others. Eleven metrics are reported, each on its own: validity, uniqueness at 1k and 10k, novelty against the training set, the share passing the medicinal-chemistry and PAINS filters used to build the dataset, two internal-diversity numbers, and four comparisons with the reference set, Frechet ChemNet Distance, similarity to a nearest neighbour, and fragment and scaffold similarity, the last four reported twice, once against each reference set. Four property distributions (molecular weight, logP, synthetic accessibility and QED) are compared by 1D Wasserstein-1 distance. There is no aggregate and no leaderboard: the README's table holds the maintainers' eight baselines, from CharRNN, VAE, AAE, JTN-VAE and LatentGAN to an n-gram model, a hidden Markov model and a combinatorial fragment generator, and everyone else reports in their own papers. MOSES scores nothing goal-directed, which is where it differs from GuacaMol, whose goal-directed half it deliberately leaves alone.

- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S1][moses-s1]
  - why: Every metric that ranks a model compares the generated set with a reference set, by Frechet ChemNet Distance between neural activations, Tanimoto similarity to the nearest reference molecule, cosine similarity of BRICS fragment and Bemis-Murcko scaffold frequencies, and Wasserstein distances between property distributions.

- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric, model-derived-metric, statistical-fit · [S1][moses-s1]
  - why: domain-metric for the chemoinformatics measures: fragment and scaffold similarity as cosine similarities of BRICS fragment and Bemis-Murcko scaffold frequencies, similarity to a nearest neighbour as a Tanimoto similarity of Morgan fingerprints, internal diversity, the share passing the medicinal-chemistry and PAINS filters, and validity as an RDKit parse. model-derived-metric for the Frechet ChemNet Distance, computed from the penultimate-layer activations of ChemNet, a released network, so its checkpoint and the FCD library version are part of the number. statistical-fit for the four property comparisons, 1D Wasserstein-1 distances between the generated and test distributions of molecular weight, logP, synthetic accessibility and QED.
  > is calculated using activations of the penultimate layer of a deep neural network ChemNet trained to predict biological activities of drugs
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model, classical-algorithm · [S4][moses-s4]
  - why: The platform is built for generative models trained on its own molecular dataset, with five neural baselines (CharRNN, VAE, AAE, JTN-VAE, LatentGAN) implemented in the package, and it enters three non-neural generators beside them in the same table.
  > We implemented several models that cover different approaches to molecular generation, such as character-level recurrent neural networks (CharRNN)

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `chemistry-materials/molecular-property-prediction` · [S1][moses-s1]
  - why: Four computed properties (molecular weight, logP, synthetic accessibility, QED) are compared, but as distributions of a generated set against a test set by a Wasserstein-1 distance; no property of a given molecule is predicted or scored.
  > we compute a 1D Wasserstein-1 distance between property distributions of generated and test sets
- `domain` not `chemistry-materials/drug-discovery-admet` · [S3][moses-s3]
  - why: The dataset is a clean-leads library and the filters remove reactive and PAINS substructures, but no absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion or toxicity property is predicted or scored; the filters are substructure rules applied when the dataset was built.

- `capability` not `optimization` · [S4][moses-s4]
  - why: No objective is stated and nothing is maximised. The paper's own framing is that it standardises the distribution-learning problem and leaves the goal-directed one to GuacaMol, so there is no objective whose value is the score.
  > We focus on standardizing metrics and data for the distribution learning problem
- `capability` not `creativity-novelty` · [S1][moses-s1]
  - why: Novelty counts the generated molecules absent from the training set and the two internal-diversity numbers measure variety, both without any usefulness criterion, which the term's exclusion test rules out; low novelty is read as overfitting rather than novelty being the goal, and the suggested general metric rewards matching the training distribution.
  > Novelty is the fraction of the generated molecules that are not present in the training set
- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S4][moses-s4]
  - why: The scaffold test set holds Bemis-Murcko scaffolds absent from train and test and every comparison metric is reported against it separately, which looks like a held-out shift. But a generative model is given no inputs, and what changes is the reference set the output is compared with, not a distribution the system was fitted to and must hold up on, which the term's inclusion test requires (review check).
  > Scaffold similarity from the training set to the scaffold test set (TestSF) is zero by design
- `evaluation_method` not `composite` · [S1][moses-s1]
  - why: No published figure combines the metrics. The paper suggests one of them, FCD against the random test set, as the single number to read for a general comparison, but that is one metric rather than a combination of several, which the term requires.

- `evaluation_method` not `constraint-check` · [S1][moses-s1]
  - why: The Filters metric does apply a battery of enumerated conditions (the medicinal-chemistry filters, PAINS, ring size, charge and atom types) in which one violation rejects a molecule. But MOSES scores a sampled set rather than items, and the reported number is the share of the 30,000 samples that pass, in the same shape as validity and uniqueness, and no item is ranked (review check).

- `designed_for_subjects` not `task-specific-supervised-model` · [S1][moses-s1]
  - why: Nothing is labelled and nothing is predicted from an input. The models are fitted to a molecular distribution and sampled from, which is the specialisation the platform tests.

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `ground_truth_source`) ground\_truth\_source held-out-labels is the nearest value for metrics computed against a held-out set of molecules that carries no labels at all; repository-tests, which GuacaMol took for the same shape, describes who computes the number rather than what the truth is. Whether the vocabulary needs a term for a reference distribution.
2. (field `data.size`) The two sources give different dataset sizes, 1,936,963 in the paper and 1,936,962 in the README, and the README gives the splits only to the nearest 100k. The CSV was not counted, so the headline size rests on the paper alone. · [S3][moses-s3]
   > The dataset contains 1,936,962 molecular structures
3. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method rejects constraint-check for the Filters metric, which really is a battery of enumerated conditions (medicinal-chemistry filters, PAINS, ring size, charge, atom types) where one violation rejects a molecule. The rejection rests on MOSES scoring a sampled set rather than ranking items; a reviewer may read the metric the other way. · [S1][moses-s1]
   > Filters is the fraction of generated molecules that pass filters applied during dataset construction
4. (field `capability`) capability carries generation-fidelity alone. distribution-shift-generalization was rejected because a generative model takes no input, so the scaffold test set shifts the reference rather than the input; if the facet is read as covering a shifted evaluation distribution, the scaffold split qualifies and the term belongs here and on moses#test-scaffolds.
5. (field `activity`) activity no-submission-channel rests on the absence of any route onto the README's table, while the repository takes pull requests and one 2020 commit on master updated a baseline's row that way (GitHub API, not a Source). Whether a repository that accepts a model and its numbers by pull request is a submission channel, which would make this self-reported and open-source-gated instead. · [S3][moses-s3]
   > Add generated samples and metrics to your repository. Run the experiment multiple times to estimate the variance of the metrics
6. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type industry-lab follows the company that led the release, not a stated holder, because no source names who holds the molecularsets organisation, and the author list spans six organisations including a pharmaceutical company and three universities. consortium and community-collective were both weighed. · [S1][moses-s1]
   > work for Insilico Medicine, a commercial artificial intelligence company
7. (field `lineage`) Identity and lineage. MOSES and GuacaMol are contemporaries that split the same field, MOSES taking distribution learning and leaving the goal-directed benchmarks to GuacaMol, and the two share FCD and the validity, uniqueness and novelty metrics. Neither derives from the other, so no lineage link is recorded; whether the pair deserves a correlates\_with or a see\_also once Metric entities exist. · [S4][moses-s4]
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
8. (field `versions`) No versions are recorded. The paper went through five arXiv versions over two years before the journal version, and the molsets package through seven releases, while the dataset file stayed dataset\_v1; v1 of the preprint was not read, so whether the metric set or the baselines changed between versions (which would be a revision under 04 S4) is unverified. · [S2][moses-s2]
   > last revised 28 Oct 2020 (this version, v5)
9. (field `data.refresh`) refresh static, while FCD depends on the ChemNet checkpoint the FCD library ships and the package pins RDKit and other dependencies; a 2021 commit on master changed a dependency constraint. Whether FCD numbers computed under different pins are comparable, which is why harness is in material\_extra.
10. (field `lifecycle`) A 2025 paper that uses the benchmark mislabels its metrics, calling SNN scaffold similarity and Scaf scaffold uniqueness, and reports Scaf as a percentage while MOSES defines it in \[0, 1\]. Its MOSES numbers are read here only as evidence of current use, not as results. · [S5][moses-s5]
   > The MOSES benchmark provides a more holistic suite, including Scaffold Similarity (SNN) and Scaffold Uniqueness (Scaf) for scaffold-level
11. (field `governance.independence_flags`) The baselines' hyperparameters were selected by random search on FCD, the metric the paper then recommends as the single general number, which couples the board's best FCD values to the metric used to tune for them. · [S4][moses-s4]
   > We used random search over multiple architectures for every model and selected the architecture that produced the best value of FCD

### 2.5 Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20) (oc20)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/oc20.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-10 · last verified 2026-11-24

*Predict DFT adsorption energies, forces and relaxed structures for adsorbates on catalyst surfaces.*

About 1.28 million DFT relaxations of small adsorbates (carbon, nitrogen and oxygen chemistries) on catalyst surfaces drawn from Materials Project bulks, with three tasks: energy and per-atom forces from a structure (S2EF), the relaxed structure from an initial one (IS2RS), and the relaxed energy from an initial structure (IS2RE). Each validation and test split has four subsplits -- in-domain, unseen adsorbates, unseen catalysts, and both -- and test ground truth is withheld. Scored by MAE and by the share of predictions within a threshold of DFT, through the maintainers' evaluation server.

**Evidence** (61 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### oc20 · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][oc20-s1]
  > The dataset and baseline models are both provided as open resources, as well as a public leader board to encourage community contributions to solve these important tasks
- `released` = 2020-10-20 · [S2][oc20-s2]
  > Submitted on 20 Oct 2020

#### oc20 · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary chemistry-materials/catalysis; secondary chemistry-materials/force-fields-potentials · [S1][oc20-s1]
  - why: The tasks model adsorbates on catalyst surfaces, and IS2RE's relaxed energy is what catalysis screening uses. S2EF scores energies and forces from structures, which is a learned potential's job.
  > This is the most common task in catalysis, as the relaxed energies are often correlated with catalyst activity and selectivity
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S1][oc20-s1]
  - why: Systems predict energies, forces and relaxed structures of adsorbate-surface systems and are scored against DFT, a reference computation.
  > Structure to Energy and Forces (S2EF ) is to take the positions of the atoms as input and predict the energy and per-atom forces as calculated by DFT
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S1][oc20-s1]
  - why: Three of the four test subsplits are drawn on purpose from adsorbates, catalysts or both that training never saw, and each is reported as its own condition.
  > These include In-Domain (sampled from the training distribution), Out-of-Domain Adsorbate (OOD Adsorbate), OOD Catalyst, and OOD Both
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit, numeric-tolerance-match · [S1][oc20-s1]
  - why: Energy and force MAE are error statistics over all predictions. EwT and EFwT count a prediction right when it falls within a fixed threshold of the DFT value.
  > The second measures the energies within a threshold (EwT) of the ground truth
- `designed_for_subjects` = scientific-surrogate-model · [S1][oc20-s1]
  - why: The entrants stand in for DFT, a physics-based solver, and are scored against what DFT computed.
  > Structure to Energy and Forces (S2EF ) is to take the positions of the atoms as input and predict the energy and per-atom forces as calculated by DFT

Considered and rejected:

- `evaluation_method` not `wet-lab-validation` · [S3][oc20-s3]
  - why: OCx24's targets are wet-lab measurements, and the taxonomy lists ocx24 as qualifying, but the term's exclusion test rules out predictions compared against previously measured data. OCx24's models are fitted to its measurements and scored on held-out ones by cross-validation; nothing an entrant predicts is taken to a laboratory (review check).
  > we explore whether models trained on experimental data using computational descriptors as input can produce results that are predictive of held out experimental data

#### oc20 · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system DimeNet++ · [S1][oc20-s1]
  > We applied three state-of-the-art graph neural network models (CGCNN, SchNet, DimeNet++) to each of these tasks
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · [S5][oc20-s5]
  - why: The training and validation data and the baselines are public, and anyone can submit test predictions to the maintainers' board.
  > In addition to the data, baseline models and code are open-sourced on our Github page
- `task` = exists true; input atom positions of an adsorbate on a catalyst surface (a structure, or an initial structure); output Per task -- the adsorption energy and per-atom forces (S2EF), the relaxed atom positions (IS2RS), or the relaxed-state energy (IS2RE).; scoring MAE of energies and forces, and the share within a threshold of DFT (EwT, EFwT; AFbT for IS2RS), on each of the four test subsplits, through the evaluation server. · [S1][oc20-s1]
  > Evaluation on the test set may only be done through the leaderboard
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = not-independently-reproducible · [S1][oc20-s1]
  - why: The headline numbers are test scores, which only the maintainers' server can compute, because it holds the DFT labels.
  > Evaluation on the test set may only be done through the leaderboard

  > This leaderboard evaluates performance on the \*\*Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20)\*\* dataset

#### oc20 · Governance and independence

- `governance.maintainer` = Open Catalyst Project (FAIR at Meta, with Carnegie Mellon University's Department of Chemical Engineering) · [S5][oc20-s5]
  - why: The project is a collaboration of the two. The code is held in Meta's facebookresearch organisation on GitHub (fairchem), and the current board in the facebook organisation on Hugging Face.
  > The Open Catalyst Project is a collaborative research effort between Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) at Meta and Carnegie Mellon University's (CMU) Department of Chemical Engineering

#### oc20 · Lifecycle and activity

- `lifecycle` = active · [S4][oc20-s4]
  - why: OC20 is scored on a new board that the maintainers' FAIR Chemistry group runs on Hugging Face. They moved it there after the EvalAI challenge closed, and its space was last changed on 2026-09-14.
  > This leaderboard evaluates performance on the \*\*Open Catalyst 2020 (OC20)\*\* dataset
- `activity` = leaderboard-live-no-round · [S4][oc20-s4]
  - why: OC20 ran challenge rounds (NeurIPS 2021 and 2022, and a 2023 adsorption-energy challenge). The EvalAI server that held them ended on 2026-01-31, and the standing board on Hugging Face takes submissions with no round open. Its runtime was RUNNING on 2026-10-10 (Hugging Face API).
  > Users are limited to \*\*5 successful submissions per month\*\* for each evaluation type
- `versions` = 3 items · [S7][oc20-s7]
  - why: The generations' ground truths are not the same quantity, so no score compares across them; OCx24's are measurements rather than DFT.
  > rather than ground truth values being DFT adsorption energies, we use DFT total energies for OC22

**Open review checks** (12):

1. independence\_flags: whether the maintainers' own models are ranked on the board.
2. refresh: whether the Hugging Face board still scores the challenge-year test sets or only the four original subsplits; if only those, static may fit better.
3. (field `governance.maintainer`) governance.maintainer names the Open Catalyst Project, which the FAIR Chemistry documentation now describes in the past tense, with the code and board held by Meta's FAIR Chemistry group. Whether the maintainer should read FAIR Chemistry (Meta), with CMU as a former partner, is for a reviewer. · [S13][oc20-s13]
   > The Open Catalyst Project was a collaborative research effort between Fundamental AI Research (FAIR) at Meta and Carnegie Mellon University's (CMU) Department of Chemical Engineering.
4. (field `versions`) The ledger models OC22 and OCx24 as versions of oc20. 04 S4 sends a derivative that is independently versioned and cited to a benchmark of its own with a lineage link, each generation has its own paper and tasks, and P1-S3-T01 called OC22 a sibling entry. The id stays oc20, and the name, description and task still describe OC20 alone. Renaming to the family (the name changes, never the id) or giving OC22 and OCx24 ids of their own is an id-allocation decision for a human.
5. (field `subsets`) held-out-server for OC22 rests on its EvalAI server alone. No source read says OC22's test labels are withheld; the OC20 paper says so for OC20 only. A reviewer should confirm it before a claim on oc20@oc22 is given held-out-server (P3-S7-T03). · [S11][oc20-s11]
   > This page hosts evaluation servers for two tasks on the Open Catalyst 2022 (OC22) dataset
6. (field `versions`) OCx24 admits neither held-out-server, which this task's verify asks of every generation, nor prospective-experiment, which P3-S7-T04 plans for its claims. Its measurements were taken before any entrant and their summaries are public, and models are scored by cross-validation on them. The test asserts the recorded absence rather than the premise. · [S12][oc20-s12]
   > Summaries of this data are all publicly available
7. (field `comparability.material_extra`) The step "attach an assay\_protocol source ref wherever ground truth is wet-lab" has no field to land in. BenchmarkVersion and Subset are closed models without one, ground\_truth\_source holds one value per benchmark, and comparability.material\_extra is per benchmark, so making assay\_protocol material would count it unknown on every OC20 and OC22 claim. The ref stands as the ocx24 version's src-arxiv-2411-11783-v1, quoted for its protocol on the OCx24 subsets; P3-S7-T04's claims can name it in EvalConditions.assay\_protocol. A version-level field, or a per-version material set, is a schema decision. · [S3][oc20-s3]
   > Parallelized screening for CO2RR and HER was performed using a modified membrane electrode assembly (MEA) setup
8. (field `evaluation_method`) taxonomy/evaluation-methods.yaml gives ocx24 as a qualifying example of wet-lab-validation, while the term's exclusion test rules out predictions compared against previously measured data, which is how OCx24 scores models. The term is rejected here; the example is for the vocabulary's maintainers.
9. (field `baselines`) The OC22 floors are read from the PDF's text, where each table is flattened column by column, as the first value of a column (the Median Baseline or IS baseline row). In the S2EF-Total table seven energy values follow eight row labels, so which row has none rests on the layout. A reader of the PDF's tables should confirm 163.424 and 160.455, 176.256 and 171.854, and 43.39 and 45.26. · [S7][oc20-s7]
   > OC22-only Median Baseline SchNet 12 DimeNet++ 13,14 ForceNet 15 SpinConv 16 PaiNN 75 GemNet-dT 17 GemNet-OC 19 163.424 7.924
10. (field `baselines`) OC20's own median baselines are in its paper's Tables 3-5, outside src-arxiv-2010-09990-v5's committed extract, so OC20 has ceilings and no floors in data/baselines/oc20.yaml; extending that extract would let them be recorded as OC22's are.
11. (field `subsets`) OCx24's R² is reported per reaction, per CO2 reduction product (H2, CO, liquid, C2H4), per feature set and per cross-validation strategy. The product has no subset and no EvalConditions field, so a claim must carry it in subset\_used. The replicate noise is in the targets' units, so it cannot anchor R² and OCx24 has no Baseline; an error metric in volts would let it be an experimental-replicate ceiling. · [S3][oc20-s3]
   > We observe an experimental standard deviation of σ = 0.050 (H2), 0.040 (CO), 0.033 (Liquid)
12. (field `versions`) The FAIR Chemistry documentation lists an OC25 dataset page beside OC20, OC22 and OCx24 (docs/catalysts/datasets/oc25.md at d733f48, listed through the GitHub API, not read). Whether it is a fourth generation of this family is open.

**Reviewer checklist** for `oc20`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.6 MassSpecGym (massspecgym)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/massspecgym.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Molecule identification from tandem mass spectra, in de novo generation, retrieval and spectrum simulation challenges.*

A benchmark and Python package from a lab at IOCB Prague and collaborators for machine learning on tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) of small molecules. Its dataset holds 231,104 labelled MS/MS spectra of about 29,000 molecules, collected from MoNA, MassBank and GNPS and from the authors' own newly measured MSnLib library, cleaned, standardised and split so that no molecule in one fold lies within a maximum-common-edge-subgraph (MCES) edit distance of 10 of a molecule in another. Three challenges are scored apart, each with a bonus variant that gives the chemical formula: de novo generation of the molecule from its spectrum (top-k accuracy, MCES and Tanimoto similarity of the best of k = 1 or 10 guesses), retrieval of the molecule from up to 256 candidates of the same mass or formula (hit rate at 1, 5 and 20, MCES of the top hit), and simulation of the spectrum from the molecule (cosine and Jensen-Shannon similarity of binned spectra, and retrieval by simulated spectra). Results tables in the repository take entries by pull request; the leaderboard site that displayed them was suspended by November 2026. In 2026 an audit by the maintainers and an MIT group found evaluation problems in at least 18 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym results and released v1.5, which re-canonicalises the SMILES strings that let models spot the true candidate, adds pretraining sets filtered against the test molecules and pins the metric implementations. Known weaknesses the sources name: shortcut learning from candidate sets, leakage through pretraining data and shared components, metric implementations that diverge across codebases, and a ranking bias in the candidate pools that v1.5 does not fix.

#### massspecgym · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary chemistry-materials/spectroscopy-interpretation; secondary chemistry-materials/molecular-property-prediction · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: Two of the three challenges, and the benchmark's stated purpose, take an MS/MS spectrum and score the molecular structure a system infers from it against the molecule that was measured.
  > The task of de novo molecular generation is to generate a molecular structure from a mass spectrum.
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: Systems predict a molecule's structure from its measured spectrum, or its spectrum from its structure, and are scored against the measured molecule or the measured spectrum (ADR-0014's term for a structure or property of a chemical system predicted from measurements of it).
  > spectrum simulation is the inverse problem of predicting an MS/MS spectrum
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: The split is built so that test molecules are structurally distant from every training molecule, by agglomerative clustering at an MCES threshold of 10, rather than by random or InChIKey-disjoint sampling, and every reported score is on those held-out structures. There is no in-distribution score beside it, which the term allows. DiffMS calls the setting out of distribution.
  > By setting the linkage distance threshold to 10, our approach ensures that no molecules have an edge edit distance of less than 10 between different data folds.
- `evaluation_method` = exact-match, domain-metric, statistical-fit · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: exact-match for de novo top-k accuracy and retrieval hit rate at k, the share of test spectra whose measured molecule is among the k outputs, each item right or wrong (the audit pins the match to the 14-character InChIKey); domain-metric for the MCES edit distance on molecular graphs and the Tanimoto similarity of Morgan fingerprints, cheminformatics measures with no meaning outside the field; statistical-fit for the cosine and Jensen-Shannon similarity between binned predicted and measured spectra.
  > We evaluate molecule retrieval using standard information retrieval metrics, as well as the molecular similarity of the top hit with the true molecule.
- `designed_for_subjects` = domain-specialist-model, scientific-surrogate-model, classical-algorithm · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: The entrants are models built for mass spectrometry, trained on MassSpecGym's training fold: the paper's MIST, DeepSets and transformer baselines and later work such as DiffMS (domain-specialist-model). In the simulation challenge the model stands in for the instrument, predicting the spectrum a measurement would give, and the paper names pseudolabeling with synthetic spectra as a use (scientific-surrogate-model; subsets cannot carry a subject override, so it is listed here). Non-learned baselines compete in the same tables: random chemical generation, random candidate ranking and a single-peak precursor m/z spectrum (classical-algorithm).
  > This baseline uses combinatorial and graph theory algorithms, drawing from statistics derived from the training data.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `chemistry-materials/generative-molecular-design` · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: The de novo challenge generates molecules, but each is scored by how close it is to the one molecule that was measured, not against a property specification it should satisfy; generating a new molecule that fits is the leaf's task, recovering a known one is not.
  > we formulate the problem as predicting a set of k graphs
- `domain` not `biology-genetics/systems-biology` · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: arXiv files the paper under q-bio and its users are computational metabolomics, but no pathway or network is modelled; the scored quantity is a small molecule's structure or spectrum, which the biology family's exclusion test sends here. Molecules of biological origin are the samples' subject, not the benchmark's.
  > we first exhaustively collected MS/MS spectra from the largest publicly available spectral libraries
- `capability` not `generation-fidelity` · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: The simulated spectrum is compared with the measured one by similarity, which reads like the term's inclusion test, but the term's exclusion test sends a predicted property or structure of a physical system scored against measurement to scientific-prediction.
  > An evaluation metric for the quality of the prediction is the cosine similarity between the predicted binned spectrum
- `capability` not `hypothesis-generation` · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: De novo returns k candidate molecules and retrieval a ranking, but the score only asks whether the one measured molecule is among them (or how close the best one is); the k guesses hedge a single determinate answer. In retrieval the candidates are supplied and only ranking is asked, which the term's exclusion test rules out.
  > we formulate the problem as predicting a set of k graphs
- `capability` not `perception` · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: The input is a measured signal, but one already reduced to a peak list of m/z and intensity pairs, noise peaks removed and intensities normalised, and the benchmark's claim is a chemical inference from it rather than recovery of structure from a raw sensory stream (review check).
  > We preprocessed the mass spectra by removing signals estimated to be instrument noise.
- `evaluation_method` not `classification-metric` · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
  - why: Hit rate at k is a ranking metric, but it is the mean of per-spectrum verdicts (is the true molecule in the top k?), which the term's exclusion test sends to exact-match.
  > The hit rate @ k ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating perfect performance

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `lineage`) CASMI against MassSpecGym, for the two entries' boundary. CASMI (the Critical Assessment of Small Molecule Identification) is a periodic blind contest, run six times since 2012, with a few hundred challenge spectra per edition and preprocessing that takes mass-spectrometry expertise; it is an edition series. MassSpecGym is a fixed, machine-learning-ready release with a public test fold of 17,556 spectra, a structure-distance split and three tasks, scored continuously by anyone. MassSpecGym grew out of a Dagstuhl seminar, not out of CASMI, and neither is a version, variant or fork of the other, so no lineage link is recorded; correlates\_with may suit if the CASMI entry finds shared methods. · [S2][massspecgym-s2]
   > However, the CASMI challenge is held only once every two years at best, limiting opportunities for continuous evaluation and benchmarking.
2. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active against under-revision. v1.5 is released (audit v1 of 2026-06-17, dataset card updated 2026-10-26), but the commit that brought it to GitHub is titled "MassSpecGym v1.5 (part 1/2)" (2026-05-08, GitHub's commit list; not a quoted Source), the README does not mention v1.5, and the results tables lack the audit's corrected rows. If a part 2 is announced, the term would be under-revision and v1.5's frozen false would stand.
3. (field `versions`) versions. v1.5 is modelled as a revision of the same items by the same maintainers (the IOCB lab's head is one of the audit's corresponding authors, and the files are in the same repositories), not as a fork by the MIT group or Enveda, who co-author the audit. breaking true rests on retrieval results that exploited the v1.0 canonicalisation collapsing under v1.5; the audit says honest de novo rankings barely move. · [S3][massspecgym-s3]
   > MassSpecGym v1.5 as a benchmark revision.
4. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The audit evidences leakage through entrants' pretraining sets, simulators and formula annotators, and finds evaluation issues in at least 18 of 26 papers. The vocabulary keeps a route evidenced for particular entrants on their claims, but when most entrants take it, high may be the better reading. · [S3][massspecgym-s3]
   > We find evaluation issues in at least 18 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in the first year of its adoption.
5. (field `description`) The audit's abstract page says 17 of 26 papers; its v2 PDF says 18. The entry quotes the PDF. · [S10][massspecgym-s10]
   > We find evaluation issues in at least 17 of 26 papers reporting MassSpecGym benchmark results in the first year of its adoption.
6. (field `activity`) activity accepting-submissions while the leaderboard site answers 503 and the results tables' newest third-party row is dated 2025-09-16. Whether the pull-request route is still being acted on was not checked (open pull requests were not read).
7. (field `execution.harness_gotcha`) Metric divergence makes table rows incomparable as listed. de\_novo\_bonus.csv gives DiffMS a top-1 MCES of 18.45, from DiffMS's paper; the audit recomputes it with the pinned myopic MCES threshold of 15 and reports 13.96. Whether the tables should be read as v1.0 results under the paper's metric code, and whether to record the audit's corrected rows as the claims of record. · [S3][massspecgym-s3]
   > to correctly use a myopic threshold of 15 instead of 100
8. (field `evaluation_method`, needs a specialist) evaluation\_method and profile. exact-match for top-k accuracy and hit rate at k (a per-item verdict on the 2D InChIKey), domain-metric for MCES and Tanimoto, statistical-fit for spectral cosine and Jensen-Shannon similarity. Spectral cosine is the standard similarity in mass spectrometry and could be read as domain-metric. The exact-match pair resolves llm-static-text, whose five prompt fields are waived, as for uspto-50k.
9. (field `capability`, needs a specialist) capability. perception is rejected because the input is a processed peak list and the claim is a chemical inference; hypothesis-generation because the k de novo guesses hedge one determinate answer. A mass spectrometrist may read the spectrum as a raw signal.
10. (field `training_data_eligibility_tiers`) training\_data\_eligibility\_tiers left empty. The board does not split entrants by what they may train on. ### 2.7 CSPBench (cspbench)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/cspbench.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*Crystal structure prediction from composition: 180 Materials Project structures, twelve distances, pool-relative ranks.*

A benchmark for crystal structure prediction (CSP) of inorganic materials: given a chemical composition, an algorithm must predict the crystal structure that composition adopts. The test set, CSP180, is 180 structures selected from the Materials Project database, 60 each of binary, ternary and quaternary compounds, spread over many space groups and crystal systems and graded by difficulty; where a composition has several known polymorphs, the prediction is compared with each and the closest counts. One prediction per composition (top-1) is scored against the ground truth by twelve distances from the authors' CSPBenchMetrics package (an energy distance computed with the M3GNet potential after relaxing both structures, and geometric and crystallographic distances such as Wyckoff-position RMSE, Sinkhorn, Chamfer and Hausdorff distances, superpose RMSD, CrystalNN fingerprint, XRD and OFM distances), and by success rates: pymatgen's StructureMatcher at fixed tolerances, space-group match, and both together. Algorithms are compared by ranking scores from 100 to 0 assigned per test structure by rank within the evaluated pool, so a score depends on which algorithms are compared. The release paper ran 13 algorithms on all 180 structures (template-based TCSP and CSPML, the ParetoCSP, GN-OA and AGOX global searches driven by the M3GNet or MEGNet potentials, and the deep-learning AlphaCrystal-II) and the DFT-based CALYPSO on a 23-structure subset. There is no leaderboard; the repository holds the test list, the predicted structures and the maintainers' own results tables. Its authors warn that the hand-picked test set carries selection bias.

### 2.8 MD17 (md17)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/md17.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-04 · last verified 2026-11-04

*Energies and forces along ab initio MD trajectories of small organic molecules, for learned force fields.*

MD17 is a set of ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories of small organic molecules, released by the sGDML group (TU Berlin's Machine Learning Group with the University of Luxembourg) with the gradient-domain machine learning (GDML) paper. Each trajectory was run at 500 K with a 0.5 fs resolution, and every frame carries the total energy and the forces on each atom at the PBE+vdW-TS level of DFT, computed with FHI-aims. The 2017 paper used eight molecules (benzene, uracil, naphthalene, aspirin, salicylic acid, malonaldehyde, ethanol, toluene); the 2018 sGDML paper added paracetamol and azobenzene, and recomputed energies and forces on the same geometries at CCSD(T) for benzene, toluene, malonaldehyde and ethanol and at CCSD for aspirin. A learned potential is trained on a small sample of one molecule's frames (1,000 in the papers; 950 for training and 50 for validation in later use) and scored by the mean absolute error of energies and force components on the other frames, per molecule. The trajectories run from about 100,000 to about a million frames; the coupled-cluster sets hold 1,500 or 2,000 structures with fixed train and test splits. Everything is public. There is no official split for the DFT trajectories and no board; results appear in papers, and the sGDML site charts published test errors by training set size. The original energies were found to be noisy, and a separately maintained recomputation, revised MD17 (rmd17), is used in its place by much later work.

  - why: Every number is an error statistic (MAE, RMSE) over continuous energies and force components against the reference labels.

  - why: The entrants are learned force fields that stand in for ab initio MD and are scored against what the reference method computed; the maintainers' chart lists only learned models (GDML, sGDML, SchNet, PhysNet, NequIP and others).

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `distribution-shift-generalization` · [S2][md17-s2]
  - why: Training and test frames are drawn from the same trajectory at the same temperature; nothing is held out by construction.
  > sampled uniformly according to the MD@DFT trajectory energy distribution

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `lineage`) Lineage. rMD17 is entered as a fork (another maintainer, another level of theory, its own DOI, splits and citations), but its makers call it a revision of MD17 and it reuses MD17 geometries, which is the revision row of 04 S4's table (same items, changed contents). If a reviewer weighs the items over the maintainer, it would be a version of md17 instead. The id rmd17 is proposed here and is not allocated; no rmd17 entry exists. · [S10][md17-s10]
   > we additionally present a revision of the MD17 where the energies and forces have been calculated using dense integration grids
2. (field `subsets`) The coupled-cluster sets are subsets of the 2018 track-set version. They come from the same group and reuse MD17 geometries, but they have their own reference, fixed splits and papers that cite them as MD17@CCSD(T); a variant with its own id is the other reading. · [S4][md17-s4]
   > We use the MD17@CCSD(T) dataset \[19\], which recalculates trajectories for molecules in MD17 using CCSD(T)
3. (field `versions`) What MD17 contains. The release paper has eight molecules and NequIP still says eight, while the sGDML site and PyTorch Geometric list ten under MD17. The 2017 and 2018 version labels are this entry's own. The 2018 FHI-aims benzene (49,863 frames) is listed separately and unexplained; the maintainers may have replaced the 2017 benzene for a fault in its energies, which no source read says. · [S1][md17-s1]
   > is a data set of eight small organic molecules, obtained from MD simulations at T=500K and computed at the PBE+vdW-TS level of electronic structure theory
4. (field `comparability`) The training set size is the condition that most changes an MD17 number (1,000; 950 + 50; 9,500 + 500; 50,000 in early papers), and no condition field holds it; the comparability comment sends it to training\_data\_policy's note. A schema field (a training-set count), or training\_data\_eligibility\_tiers keyed by size, would make it checkable. No tiers are recorded, as no board or rule splits entrants. · [S6][md17-s6]
   > { "x": 15000, "y": 0.161 }, { "x": 50000, "y": 0.0468 }
5. (field `capability`) sample-efficiency rests on the release paper's claim and its samples-to-target figure, the conventional 1,000-frame budget and the coupled-cluster sets' fixed training split; the DFT trajectories themselves fix no budget, which the term's inclusion test asks for.
6. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active. PyTorch Geometric and NequIP describe the original DFT labels as noisy, and much current DFT-molecule use has moved to rMD17; the coupled-cluster sets and the MD17-10k protocol are still used. superseded may fit the DFT trajectories. · [S8][md17-s8]
   > This version of the dataset was found to suffer from high numerical noise.
7. (field `lifecycle`) Current-use evidence is the MD-ET paper, one of whose authors co-wrote both MD17 papers; the independent NequIP paper is from 2021. A fully independent 2025-2026 result on original MD17 or the coupled-cluster sets was not found in the time spent; 2025-2026 results on rMD17 count for the fork.
8. (field `governance.submission_process`) submission\_process literature-only, although the maintainers keep per-dataset charts of others' published errors with their own models highlighted. It is neither maintainer-run (they did not run the models) nor self-reported (no channel). Whether the charts mix original-MD17 and rMD17 numbers, or runs at 950 and 1,000 frames under one x value, was not checked. · [S5][md17-s5]
   > Test errors published for this dataset
9. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. Beyond pretraining exposure (evidence for one model and one molecule), test frames are time-correlated with training frames of the same trajectory; the facet has no term for that within-benchmark leakage, and high may fit better. · [S9][md17-s9]
   > they are not guaranteed to be independent samples
10. (field `data.size`) Sizes disagree in places. The release paper gives 150 k to nearly 1 M frames while the site lists uracil at 133,770, and toluene CCSD(T) is 1,500 on the site and 1,501 in PyTorch Geometric. The supplements' tables, which would settle them, were not read. · [S2][md17-s2]
   > These data sets range in size from 150 k to nearly 1 M conformational geometries with a resolution of 0.5 fs
11. (field `data.dataset_licence`) dataset\_licence null. No licence was found on the site or in the papers' text; the supplements and quantum-machine.org were not read. PyTorch Geometric redistributes the files.

- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right

- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved

### 2.9 TDC ADMET Benchmark Group (tdc-admet)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/tdc-admet.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*22 small-molecule ADMET prediction tasks on fixed scaffold splits, each with its own TDC leaderboard.*

The Therapeutics Data Commons' benchmark group for the absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) of small molecules: 22 datasets taken from published studies, from Caco-2 permeability and CYP450 inhibition to hERG blockade and drug-induced liver injury, of 475 to 13,130 compounds each. Every dataset has one fixed scaffold split that holds out 20% of its compounds for test. Entrants train on the rest, redrawing the train and validation sets under at least five seeds, and report the mean and standard deviation over those runs. Nine regression tasks are scored by MAE or, where the property depends on more than chemical structure, by Spearman correlation; 13 binary tasks by AUROC, or AUPRC where positives are rare. Each dataset has its own leaderboard on tdcommons.ai and no group-wide score is published. The PyTDC package returns the test labels with the data, entrants compute their own scores with its evaluator and send them through a form. Known weaknesses the sources name: the test sets have been public since 2021, so tuning on them can lift a model's rank, and a 2026 audit could reproduce only three of the top-ranked models.

#### tdc-admet · Identity and id

#### tdc-admet · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary chemistry-materials/drug-discovery-admet · [S1][tdc-admet-s1]
  - why: Every one of the 22 tasks predicts an ADMET property of a small molecule from its structure, and the site groups them under absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity.
  > An ML model that could accurately predict all ADMET properties using structural information of compounds would be greatly valuable.
- `capability` = scientific-prediction · [S4][tdc-admet-s4]
  - why: Systems predict measured pharmacokinetic and toxicity properties of compounds from their structure and are scored against the experimental values.
  > the ADME learning task aims to predict experimental properties of individual compounds
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S4][tdc-admet-s4]
  - why: Every test set is a scaffold split, held out so that the test compounds are structurally distant from the training compounds, and the score on it is the one the board ranks.
  > ADMET prediction requires a model to generalize to a set of unseen drugs that are structurally distant to the known drug set.
- `evaluation_method` = statistical-fit, classification-metric · [S1][tdc-admet-s1]
  - why: The nine regression tasks are scored by MAE or Spearman correlation against measured values (statistical-fit); the 13 binary tasks by AUROC or AUPRC against labels (classification-metric).
  > Spearman's correlation coefficient is used for benchmarks that depend on factors beyond the chemical structure.
- `designed_for_subjects` = scientific-surrogate-model · [S4][tdc-admet-s4]

**Open review checks** (9):

1. (field `name`) The entry is the ADMET Benchmark Group alone. TDC's other benchmark groups, listed beside it in the site's menu, have their own tasks, splits and boards and would be entries of their own; TDC as a platform is not one. · [S1][tdc-admet-s1]
   > ADMET Group DrugCombo Group Docking Group DTI DG Group Single-cell DTI Group
2. (field `activity`) activity accepting-submissions rests on the guidelines' standing invitation. The form needs a Google sign-in and could not be checked, and the boards have not changed since 2025-07-13; if the form is closed, no-submission-channel or unknown fits better. · [S11][tdc-admet-s11]
   > "date":"2025-07-13T17:44:04Z"},"message":"update leaderboard"
3. (field `governance.submission_process`) submission\_process self-reported rests on no stated check and on a row that carries the docs' example output. The guidelines' FAIR4RS statement could be read as a code-release condition (open-source-gated); most rows link code and a paper, which the form asks for. · [S6][tdc-admet-s6]
   > we apply FAIR4RS principles and implementation guidelines to all software and ML tools included in TDC leaderboards
4. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium. The audit traces leakage in three top-ranked entrants and shows that tuning on the public test sets lifts rank; whether that is a benchmark-level route (high) or entrant-level (medium, as recorded) is a judgement. · [S5][tdc-admet-s5]
   > Our deliberately overfitted models entered the top-3 in 10 out of 22 end points
5. (field `data.refresh`) refresh versioned-releases against the audit's statement that TDC has no data set versioning. The Dataverse record shows the group's file unchanged since 2021-02-26; rolling-live would fit if the evaluator or the loader's processing changed scores between PyTDC releases. · [S5][tdc-admet-s5]
   > The platform does not provide fixed data set releases, version identifiers, check sums or detailed changelogs
6. (field `designed_for_subjects`, needs a specialist) designed\_for\_subjects scientific-surrogate-model, because the entrants emulate assay and in vivo measurements; domain-specialist-model is the alternative, as for ProteinGym.
7. (field `capability`, needs a specialist) distribution-shift-generalization rests on the scaffold split alone. No in-distribution score is reported beside it, which the term allows, and whether a scaffold split counts as a deliberately shifted distribution is a cheminformatics judgement.
8. (field `aggregation_policy`) aggregation\_policy none-by-design. The maintainers publish no group score and accept single-dataset submissions, but the guidelines encourage whole-group submissions, and others average ranks across the boards; unknown or community-aggregate are the alternatives.
9. (field `governance.independence_flags`) Whether the release paper's baselines, listed with a maintainer as contact, count as maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark, as RoboCasa's baseline rows do. · [S7][tdc-admet-s7]
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]

### 2.10 CACHE Challenges (cache-challenges)

`data/benchmarks/chemistry-materials/cache-challenges.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Prospective hit-finding: teams nominate compounds for a protein target, and the organisers buy and assay them.*

A series of prospective hit-finding competitions, launched by the Structural Genomics Consortium (SGC) in 2021 and stewarded by the non-profit Conscience since 2024. Each challenge names one protein target of biological or pharmaceutical interest, from LRRK2's WD40 domain (Parkinson's disease) and two SARS-CoV-2 proteins to a GPCR and parts of E3 ligases. Teams selected by application and double-blind peer review use computational workflows (docking, physics-based scoring, machine learning, generative design, often with chemists' judgement) to nominate up to 100 purchasable compounds; the organisers buy them, mostly from Enamine, and test them in binding assays with orthogonal confirmation. Teams whose compounds show activity nominate up to 50 analogues in a second, hit-expansion round, and every team also predicts the actives in the pooled first-round library. An independent Hit Evaluation Committee of industry experts scores each confirmed hit on its measured activity, its chemistry and novelty, and its analogues, and workflows are compared on those scores. All structures and assay data are released after each challenge. Confirmed hits are rare: seven of the 1,955 compounds tested in Challenge #1, and 0.7% of Challenge #2's. Eight challenges were announced from 2021 to 2026; assays and activity thresholds differ by target, so scores do not compare across challenges.
